note.text:
In a metal, each atom releases its outer (valence) electrons. The atoms become positive ions arranged in a regular lattice, and the released electrons move freely among them: a 'sea' of delocalised electrons.
The metallic bond is the attraction between the positive ions and the sea of electrons.
• Sodium gives 1 electron per atom, magnesium 2, aluminium 3: more delocalised electrons and higher ion charge give a stronger bond (aluminium melts higher than sodium).
• The bond is not between particular pairs of atoms: it holds the whole lattice together.

sections.heading: Atoms that give up electrons
sections.text:
Metal atoms have only {1}, {2} or {3} outer electrons, held loosely. In a piece of metal, every atom lets its outer electrons go.
The atoms become positive ions, packed tightly in a regular pattern (a lattice). The released electrons are free to move anywhere in the metal: they are delocalised.

sections.heading: The sea of electrons
sections.text:
Picture rows of positive ions sitting in a 'sea' of moving electrons. The ions are attracted to the negative sea all around them.
This attraction is the metallic bond. It does not join particular pairs of atoms; it holds the whole lattice together, which is why metals are strong.

sections.heading: Stronger and weaker metallic bonds
sections.text:
The more electrons each atom puts into the sea, and the higher the charge on the ions, the stronger the bonding.
• Sodium (Na⁺, {1} electron each) is soft and melts at {98} °C.
• Magnesium (Mg²⁺, {2} each) melts at {650} °C.
• Aluminium (Al³⁺, {3} each) melts at {660} °C.

mistake.wrong: A metal is held together by negative ions
mistake.right: A metal has positive ions held by a sea of free electrons
mistake.why: Metal atoms lose electrons; there are no negative ions in a pure metal.

worked_example.problem: Describe the bonding in magnesium (atomic number {z}).
steps: It becomes Mg²⁺ ions in a regular lattice.
The released electrons move freely between the ions; the ions are held by attraction to this sea of electrons.
worked_example.answer: Mg²⁺ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons

cards.idea: Metal atoms release their outer electrons into a shared sea.
The metallic bond: positive ions attracted to delocalised electrons.
example: The electrons are not attached to any one ion.

cards.idea: More delocalised electrons per atom: a stronger metallic bond.

pick.q: Aluminium (660 °C) melts at a higher temperature than sodium (98 °C). Why?
pick.r: Each Al atom gives 3 electrons and forms Al³⁺, so the attraction is stronger
e: Aluminium is a metal: metallic bonding.
Sodium gives only 1 electron per atom.
Metals are not molecular.
pick.y: More electrons in the sea and higher charge on the ions: stronger metallic bonding.

pick.q: Which metal would you expect to have the strongest metallic bonding?
e: Sodium gives 1 electron per atom.
Potassium gives 1 and has larger ions.
Lithium gives 1 electron per atom.

pick.q: Why are metal ions not pushed apart, even though they are all positive?
pick.r: The sea of electrons between them holds them together
w: They are held by negative ions
e: They are positive ions.
The electrons are not in fixed pairs.
There are no negative ions in a pure metal.
pick.y: The negative electron sea attracts all the ions.
